panels.title: Recent quality upgrades
panels.description:
Files replaced by a **different** quality, newest first.

An upgrade is two events at the same instant: the old file deleted with reason `Upgrade`, and the new
one imported. The same quality on both sides means it was a custom-format score upgrade, not a
resolution change.

**Colours follow the download policy, not the resolution:**
🔵 4K · 🟢 what the TV direct-plays (Bluray/WEB 1080p) · 🟠 works but wastes space (Remux-1080p, 720p)
· 🔴 unwanted (BR-DISK, cams, SD)

panels.title: Upgrades tracked
panels.description:
How many upgrades are currently being exposed. The exporter keeps only the most recent ones, so
this is a window, not a lifetime count.

panels.title: Upgraded in the last 7 days
panels.description: Upgrades whose timestamp falls inside the last week, out of the window the exporter keeps.

panels.title: Stuck on a bad quality
panels.description:
Titles whose current file is a quality the download policy rejects: cams, telesyncs, SD, DVD,
BR-DISK.

Worth checking by hand, because Radarr does not always treat these as upgradable. A quality that is
not even allowed in the profile has no rank to compare against, so it can sit below the cutoff
without ever appearing in the upgrade list.

panels.title: Waiting on Radarr
panels.description:
Everything Radarr is waiting for, and what it is waiting for.

| Kind | Meaning |
| :--- | :--- |
| 🔵 `downloading` | in the queue right now. **Expected** is the ETA, or `stalled` when no bytes have moved |
| 🟠 `missing` | monitored with no file at all: cannot be watched |
| 🟢 `upgrade` | watchable, but below the profile cutoff |

**Now** is the quality on disk, 🔴 `none` when there is no file.

**Expected** is the honest half of "when". Nobody can say when someone uploads a good release, but
two things are knowable:

- `in cinemas, no digital date` — the film has no home release yet, so no amount of searching will
  find a better one
- `out, waiting for a good release` — it exists in the world, so this is down to an indexer carrying
  it. The nightly cutoff search asks about exactly this list

panels.title: Reachable
panels.description:
Whether the exporter can talk to qBittorrent's WebUI at all. Down means the metrics on this row
are stale, not that the torrents stopped.

panels.title: Torrents in error
panels.description:
Torrents in `error` or `missingFiles`: the data is unreadable, or it was moved or deleted from
under qBittorrent. These never recover on their own.

panels.title: Stalled downloads
panels.description:
Torrents that want to download but find no seeds. One stalled for hours usually means the
release is dead: blocklist it in Radarr so it grabs a different one instead of retrying the same.

panels.title: Torrents
panels.description:
**What the states mean**

| State | Meaning |
| :--- | :--- |
| `downloading` | pulling data right now |
| `metaDL` | fetching the .torrent metadata (magnet just added) |
| `stalledDL` | wants to download but finds no seeds: stuck |
| `queuedDL` | waiting for a download slot |
| `uploading` | sending data to someone right now |
| `stalledUP` | seeding, but nobody is downloading from you. Normal for old titles |
| `queuedUP` | finished, waiting its turn to seed. **Not seeding at all** |
| `pausedUP` / `stoppedUP` | stopped on purpose, or its share limit was reached |
| `checkingUP` / `checkingDL` | verifying pieces against the disk |
| `moving` | being moved between folders |
| `error` / `missingFiles` | broken: the data is unreadable or gone |

Many torrents sitting in `queuedUP` means qBittorrent's active-torrent limit is lower than the number
of torrents, so it is rotating them. Queued time does not count towards a share limit, so those
torrents also take longer to retire themselves.

panels.description:

panels.title: Torrents by state over time
panels.description:
How the mix of states moves. What to read into it:

- `queuedUP` above zero means the active-torrent limit is below the number of torrents
- `stalledUP` falling means torrents are reaching their share limit and stopping, which is the
  library cleaning itself up
- `stalledDL` that never clears is a dead release

panels.title: Storage used
panels.description: % of the /mnt/data pool in use. Max is the pool's real total capacity, not a guess — turns orange/red as it fills up.

panels.title: Free space
panels.description: Absolute free space left on the /mnt/data pool: the gauge only shows the percentage.

panels.title: Disk by quality
panels.description:
Space per quality, taken from Radarr, so the quality is the one it recorded and not a guess from
the filename.

Same colours as the upgrades table: 🔵 4K · 🟢 good · 🟠 wasteful · 🔴 unwanted.

panels.title: Disk usage by folder
panels.description:
Top-level folders on the data disk, from `du`, which counts each inode once per run. A hardlinked
file therefore lands in whichever folder du walks first rather than being counted in both.

panels.title: Biggest titles (top 20)
panels.description:
Largest titles in the library, with the quality that explains the size. Radarr is the source, so
each imported file is counted once even when it is hardlinked to a torrent in downloads/.

panels.title: Largest files on disk
panels.description:
Largest files on the data disk, one line per inode, taken from the disk rather than from Radarr.

That is the point of having it next to the panel above: it also shows files Radarr knows nothing
about, such as downloads that were never imported or were replaced by a better release.

Labels are filenames; the full paths are in the table below.

panels.title: Largest files on disk, full paths
panels.description:
The same files as the panel above, with their full path, and filtered by the **Folder** dropdown.

Written periodically by `disk-usage-metrics.sh`, so a file deleted moments ago can still appear here
until the next run.

One line per inode: the *arrs hardlink on import, so a grabbed file and its library copy are the same
bytes under two paths. Counting both would double the footer total.

panels.title: Audio languages per title
panels.description:
Every film in Radarr and the audio languages its file carries, straight from Radarr's own
naming (no translation table here).

The `Audio language` picker at the top filters the list: leave it on All to see the whole
library with every language each film has, or pick one to get only the films that have it.
A film with several languages is one series per language underneath, which is what makes the
filter work; the grouping collapses it back to one row per film.

Quality wears the same colours as "Stuck on a bad quality" above, so a 2160p reads blue in
both places. That mapping is copied from that panel, not reinvented here.

panels.title: Films per language
panels.description:
How many films carry each audio language. Counts every film that has the track, so a film
with five languages is counted under all five and the total is larger than the library.

Eight languages have a hue of their own; the rest share grey. Eighteen distinguishable hues
do not exist, and a palette that pretends otherwise is read as noise. The eight are pinned by
name rather than by rank, so a language keeps its colour as the library grows.
